title: Global mapping of flux and microbial sources for oceanic N_2O

paper_content.abstract: The ocean is the largest source of N2O emissions from global aquatic ecosystems. However, the N2O production–consumption mechanism and microbial spatial distribution are still unclear. Our study established a bottom-up model based on the source‒sink boundary and the microbial sources of N2O. A high-resolution (0.1°) global distribution of oceanic N2O was depicted, confirmed by approximately 150,000 surface measurements. The microbial N2O flux is 2.9 Tg/yr N-N2O, with the oxygen-deficient zones (ODZs) disproportionately accounting for more than half of the total emission. High primary productivity, sharp oxyclines, and shallow emission depths caused the ODZs to be N2O hotspots. Geographically, ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA, 1.0 Tg) are the most widely distributed contributors to N2O emissions in the ocean, completely overtaking ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB). Heterotrophic denitrification, mainly occurring in ODZs, contributes the most (1.6 Tg) to N2O emissions. Overall, this study offers a bottom-up framework for understanding microbial source-sink mechanism in the ocean.
paper_content.introduction:
Nitrous oxide (N2O), one of the most important greenhouse gases and the greatest human-related threat to the ozone layer, has increased substantially, by over 23%, since preindustrial times1. As a long-lived (116±9 years) greenhouse gas, nitrous oxide (N2O) is 265-298 times higher than CO2 in the global warming potential on a 100-year timescale2. Oceans are among Earth’s largest sources of N2O emissions, second only to natural soils and agriculture (IPCC). Although the amount of oceanic emissions has been well constrained3,4, current estimates are usually based on air‒sea flux (ΔpN2O)3,5 or simple semi-empirical equations6–8; thus, the N2O production‒consumption mechanism and spatial distribution of microbial N2O sources in oxygen-stratified oceans are still unclear9,10.

N2O emissions are microbially driven and highly oxygen sensitive in the ocean, leading to high heterogeneity in ΔpN2O. However, the coverage of ΔpN2O data is generally limited and in broad ranges, uncertainties inevitably widen when extrapolating ΔpN2O data to the global scale3. Moreover, sources and sinks coexist in the oxygen-stratified ocean11–13, and surface-based measurements cannot reflect the production and consumption of N2O in the deep layers. Therefore, how N2O is emitted from the ocean, how deep the source‒sink boundary is, and how it evolves cannot be explained, especially under the effects of increased stratification and deoxygenation expansion14. Most quantitative analyses of N2O microbial sources are conducted at the regional scale11,12 or on the basis of semi empirical equations of nitrification and denitrification6–8,10, which do not consider the niche separation of N2O-related microbial processes in different ecological niches6–8. For example, ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA) have greater affinity for substrates and compete for ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB) in the NH4+-limited ocean15,16. Nevertheless, several studies have reported the contribution of AOB to marine N2O emissions via nitrifier denitrification (NDN)17. Under hypoxic or anoxic conditions, N2O is produced as an intermediate during heterotrophic denitrification (HDN), with organic matter as the electron donor10,18. However, the quantification and spatial distributions of these microbes with respect to N2O emissions have not been well depicted in the ocean9,10.

In this study, we established a bottom-up model based on the source‒sink boundary and the microbial sources of marine N2O. Extensive literature research has been conducted to obtain the geochemical profiles of DO and N2O concentrations and isotopic signatures (δ15NBulk, δ18O and δ15NSP) at in situ locations (approximately 1000 lines of data), along with the isotopic characteristic values for each N2O production pathway (i.e., AOA, AOB, HDN, and NDN). We identified the source‒sink boundary of N2O via global oxygen stratification (up to 5000 m) in the water column. FRAME model was then used to quantify the specific microbial contributions to N2O emissions and N2O reduction degree19. Finally, the ammoxidation (ammonia oxidation) flux, N2O yield during ammoxidation (NO-N/NH4+-N), and quantified N2O microbial sources and fraction of residual unreduced N2O (rN2O) were combined as constraints to accurately estimate global marine N2O emissions. The results have been confirmed by a large compilation of N2O in situ measurements (approximately 150,000)3. Overall, our results present a detailed spatial distribution of marine N2O emissions with a source‒sink mechanism and quantified microbial sources.
paper_content.results:
N2O source‒sink boundary in the ocean
Due to the limit of light, the decomposition of organic matter or the poor mixing and ventilation, the ocean is oxygen-stratified. Earlier studies have revealed maximum N2O concentration in the oxygen minimum zones of the ocean11,20,21. N2O has a perfect mirror-image relationship with DO and reaches its highest concentration at the lowest amount of dissolved oxygen (Supplementary Figs. 2–11)11,22. Regardless of the upwelling, the source‒sink boundary of N2O, below which the water column does not contribute to N2O emissions, was identified by a comprehensive grid-by-grid (0.1°) traversal of DO up to 5000 m in the ocean (Fig. 1). In oxygen-deficient zones (ODZs), DO decreases to anaerobic levels (minimum O2 ≤10 μM) at shallower depths (387.9 m on average, Fig. 1b). In addition to the three major ODZs (Fig. 1c), namely, the Eastern Tropical North Pacific (ETNP), Eastern Tropical South Pacific (ETSP), and Arabian Sea, we also found some sporadic ODZs in the North Pacific Ocean, indicating the potential hotspots of N2O emissions. The upper oxycline (UO), with a N2O peak at the oxic‒anoxic interface (Supplementary Fig. 2–5), is the engine driving N2O diffusion to the mixed layer (ML). The sharp oxycline creates favorable conditions for incomplete denitrification and nitrification with high N2O yields, driving high supersaturation and fluxes of N2O at the surface11,23. Additionally, a stable proportionality of 0.45 and 2.58 for the plot of δ18O versus δ15NBulk (R2=0.52, Supplementary Fig. 12) was observed above and below the source‒sink boundary, respectively. In general, a strong correlation with slopes of 2.6 is evident when reduction process dominates, which contrasts from a slope of <1 commonly observed for mixing of N2O production and atmospheric N2O24–26. The slope of 0.45 proved the production, mixing and emission of N2O in the source part. In contrast, the slope of 2.58 confirmed the significant net N2O consumption in the ODZ core. Thereby the N2O concentrations simultaneously decreased to 0 at the middle of ODZ core (Fig. 1a). Furthermore, the isotopic composition of N2O in the ODZ core is significantly different from that in the source layer, further ruling out vertical exchange with the source layer. Therefore, the long-term and large-scale anaerobic areas ensure net N2O consumption in the ODZ core, which acts as the sink of N2O. In other oceans, the N2O peak was also observed at the lowest point of oxygen (Supplementary Fig. 6–11), although the boundary DO ranged from 10 μM to more than 300 μM (Fig. 1c). In the vast North Pacific Ocean and equatorial regions, the boundary DO is less than 50 μM, accompanied by a shallow boundary depth (less than 1000 m), favouring excessive N2O production and emission. A deeper source‒sink boundary has been found in the North Atlantic and Southern Oceans. The boundary DO increased to more than 300 μM with the boundary depth reaching 2000 m. Overall, the source‒sink boundary of N2O in the ocean was identified (Fig. 1), and the water column below the source‒sink boundary does not contribute to atmospheric emissions; therefore, it was excluded from the remainder of this study.

Microbial processes governing N2O production and consumption
To quantify the microbial sources of N2O and the fraction of residual unreduced N2O (rN2O) in the source part, the isotopic N2O values obtained from Keeling plot (Supplementary Figs. 13–22), the corrected isotope signatures of the microbial sources (Supplementary Table 1-2), and the isotopocule fractionation constants (i.e., εN: −15.4±4.7, εO: −7.1±2.1, and εSP: −5.9±1.4) for N2O reduction process were input to the model FRAME (Supplementary Fig. 23). In this study, four common microbial sources (HDN, NDN, AOB, AOA) and rN2O was quantified (Supplementary Fig. 24, Supplementary Table 3). The linear regression relationships between N2O microbial sources and boundary DO were uniformly adopted for extrapolation to global oceans (Supplementary Fig. 25, Fig. 2).

The primary productivity, substrate availability, boundary depth, and DO together determine the niche distribution of each N-cycling microorganism in the ocean. AOA dominate the nitrification pathway, contributing 34.1% of the N2O in the ocean (Table 1), which is the dominant N2O production pathway in the North Atlantic and Southern Oceans. Although both of them are chemoautotrophic processes, AOA have a greater affinity for NH4+ and oxygen20,22,27. Thereby, AOA exceeds AOB in NH4+-limited oceans with sharp oxyclines, while the contribution of AOB increases in high-latitude regions with high-oxygen (e.g., the Arctic Ocean and Antarctic Oceans). The isotopic signatures of N2O in the Arctic Ocean have proved the important role of both AOA and AOB to N2O productions12. In the ODZs, AOB are completely depleted (2.2%) because of phytoplankton competition, rapidly decreasing oxygen gradients, and surface light inhibition derived from shallow boundary depths. HDN, fueled by organic matter exported from the photic zone, is the dominant N2O production pathway in the North Pacific Ocean and equatorial regions. It further increases to 63.3% in ODZs because the abundant organic electron donors and sharp oxyclines create favorable conditions for incomplete denitrification. Notably, the contribution of denitrification is still considerable even if DO does not reach the anaerobic level in the open ocean. It is possibly associated with organic particles; the interior of sinking particles can afford a low-DO microenvironment20. On a global scale (Fig. 2), the contribution of denitrification (HDN+NDN) to N2O emissions is 61.1% (Table 1), nearly two-fold greater than that of nitrification (AOA+AOB). HDN is the first contributor to oceanic N2O emission, whereas AOA are the most widely distributed contributor in the ocean.

Global distribution of N2O flux in the ocean
To obtain the global N2O flux in a year scale (Tg N2O-N/yr), we first calculated the N2O emissions by AOA (N2OAOA) in each grid on the basis of the ammoxidation flux (ammonia oxidation amount in a year scale), N2O yield during ammoxidation (NO-N/NH4+-N), and the fraction of residual unreduced N2O (rN2O, Supplementary Fig. 25e). The total N2O flux was then obtained according to its proportion to total production in each grid (e.g., N2OAOA/fAOA; see Methods for details). It is worth noting that the fraction of residual unreduced N2O (rN2O) determines the net emission of N2O. We established the empirical formula between the rN2O and the boundary DO (Supplementary Fig. 25e). As the boundary DO rises, there is initially an increase in rN2O, followed by a subsequent decline. In ODZs with micro-oxic environment, the N2O production and reduction are both active. As the boundary DO increases, the N2O reduction is prior to be inhibited as nitrous oxide reductase (nos) is the most O2 sensitive denitrifying enzyme28, leading to the increase of rN2O. However, the data obtained in the shallow Arctic Ocean and off the coast of Antarctica gave rN2O values as low as 20% in spite of high boundary DO (Supplementary Fig. 25e)3,12,29. This implies that a significant portion of the N2O produced in situ or diffused from the atmosphere is reduced by denitrification in sediments12.

The annual N2O flux is 2.9 Tg/yr N-N2O (Fig. 3, Table 1), the distribution of which is in line with primary production pulses. On average, the turnover rate of phytoplankton (growth, death, and mineralization) is 45 times a year30, providing never-ending NH4+, NO3-, and organic matter for the continuous production of N2O via nitrification and denitrification. Furthermore, the decay of phytoplankton creates the anaerobic environment for the significant production of N2O. Therefore, the oceans around the equator contribute the most to marine N2O emissions, where ODZs disproportionately account for more than half of N2O emissions (1.6 Tg N-N2O) with only 0.1–0.2% of the ocean volume31. A higher flux of N2O has also been observed in other oceans with high primary productivity, e.g., the Gulf of Guinea, Bay of Bengal, Gulf of Mexico, and Indonesia. In contrast, slight supersaturation and occasional undersaturation are predicted in the open Arctic Ocean and Southern Ocean, with limits on light and temperature at high latitudes. With respect to microbial sources (Table 1), the contribution of denitrification is almost twofold greater than that of nitrification. Traditional HDN is the largest contributor (1.6 Tg) to N2O emissions in the ocean, which mainly occurs in ODZs (1.0 Tg). AOA are the most widely distributed contributors (1.0 Tg) in the NH4+-limited ocean and completely overcome AOB (0.1 Tg) to N2O emissions.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript presents modelling of the N2O ocean flux based mostly on literature data of several ocean profiles including geochemical data and N2O isotopocules. The approach is innovative and tries to apply most up-to-date interpretation strategies to determine the special distribution of ocean N2O flux and to identify and quantify the microbial N2O production pathways. This is a very challenging task, the idea is very interesting but in my opinion the results evaluation and presentation is not acceptable. The calculation methods applied can not be verified due to lack of proper description, it is not clear how the authors came to most of their results.
There are many unclear point in the manuscript, I will mostly concentrate on my expertise – N2O modelling, which I cannot follow in many points, although I am working with such modelling and the applied approaches should be perfectly clear to me. And unfortunately they are not. It can be due to improper application of these methods or due to minimal description of the applied calculations. I understand it might have been forced by the requirements of this journal, but then I think it is not the proper journal to describe such a complex combination of approaches. I think you should chose a journal with unlimited length of articles, and where method can be described before results. In the current form your manuscript reads very difficult, because you use a few of advanced evaluation methods which are not introduced but discussed and the reader is quickly lost. I think it shouldn’t be published this way.
When describing the evaluation method there are many important points missing, even if you have to keep it short you have to be precise, especially about methods you are using. You should always cite the original work presenting the method and shortly explain how it is working, eg. For your isotope map approach, mentioned in Scenario 1 you do not even cite the source paper of this. In Scenario 2 you try to make the multi-isotope mixing applying the SIMMR model, where you have to ignore or very much simplify the N2O reduction process. I have also been trying to work with this approach, unsuccessfully, because you cannot really compute fractionation process with this model. This is why we have developed another tool where you can simultaneously calculate mixing proportions and fractionation processes (Lewicki et al., 2022). This is an easy-to-use software, which even do not require any programming skills: https://malewick.github.io/frame/ . Applying this tool would save you a lot of inconsistencies in your descriptions, especially with the case of N2O reduction, which I really do not understand how you have determined, why you apply the mean value of 0.72, if you assume it is stable for all the data points you use.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
General comments
This paper reports detailed estimates of oceanic N2O flux and relative contributions of biological N2O production processes using published data of N2O isotope ratios, basic physical and chemical oceanic parameters, and a three-dimensional diffusion and reaction model. Because the ocean is one of the major sources of N2O, a potent greenhouse gas as well as a stratospheric ozone depleting gas, improving the estimates of N2O flux and understanding the key N2O production mechanisms would be beneficial in predicting future increases or decreases in N2O concentrations.
The strength of this paper is that the N2O flux was estimated with high spatial resolution using relatively basic parameters such as temperature, dissolved oxygen, particular organic nitrogen with the aid of N2O isotope ratios that provide a history of microbial production and consumption processes. The model-predicted N2O flux well reproduces spatial gradient found by observations.
However, this paper has several shortcomings. First, the developed method for calculating the N2O flux depends on source partitioning based on isotopic measurements that cover only a few specific regions in the global ocean. For example, the authors used isotopic data from only eastern parts of the North and South Pacific. I think there have been several reports on other parts of the Pacific. Although the authors argue that relative contribution of nitrification and DO at the “source-sink” boundary has a linear relationship, it is not necessarily proven by the data presented in Figure S20. I think examination of more data from other regions are necessary.
Second, the authors’ assumption that N2O dissolved in the depths shallower than the “source-sink” boundary is a simple mixture of two components, N2O of atmospheric origin and that produced near the boundary, is a crude one that ignores detailed analysis of previous studies. For example, Kelly et al. (2021) identified two sources between the surface and the near-surface N2O maximum in their Keeling plot analysis of isotopic data obtained in the ETNP results. Toyoda et al. (2002) also noted that there are two different N2O sources between the surface and N2O maximum in the western North Pacific, although the latter work is not referred in the present manuscript. In addition to these points, I have a concern that previous efforts on observations and interpretation of oceanic N2O are not fully acknowledged in this manuscript.
Third, it is not clear whether the authors assume the occurrence of N2O reduction even in the shallower seawater above the “source-sink” boundary. I was not able to understand why they uniformly used rN2O = 0.72 to estimate isotopic signature of N2O produced by microbial processes even though they seem to define the upper layer as source region.
Fourth, uncertainty of the estimated contributions from each microbial process is not shown, and explanation of the isotope-based source partitioning procedure is missing both in text and supporting materials. I cannot evaluate the accuracy of the estimation.
In summary, I do not recommend the publication of this paper in its present form. I encourage the authors to address the issue above and specific points below.
Specific comments
L37 & 62. I cannot understand how “oxygen is stratified”, although seawater can be stratified because of its density.
L41–45. It seems that the authors consider N2O in the deep waters below the mixed layer diffuses upward and is eventually emitted to the atmosphere. It is difficult to detect such a process within the typical time scale of the surface measurements. If ocean stratification is increased, vertical diffusion would be further suppressed. It would be better to clarify the time scale considered in this study.
L47. I think refs #10 & #11 used N2O isotopes, not “semiempirical equations of nitrification and denitrification”.
L52–54. The cited references reported the potential significance of autotrophic denitrification in the limited oceanic region such as coastal sea floor and the Black Sea, which are hardly considered in the present study.
L58–62. This statement could be misleading as if the authors had made the field work and research. Cite appropriate studies, and briefly review the knowledge obtained by them. Also, as far as I know, no study reported isotopic signatures of N2O produced by ADN.
L63. Did the authors use only d15NSP values out of the three isotope parameters? Describe the details of the model.
L65. It seems that the authors use “ammoxidation” as a contradiction of ammonia oxidation. I think this term is not always in common use. Define it at the first use. Also, replace “stoichiometric” with other appropriate word. As described by the authors elsewhere, amount of microbially produced N2O is often variable and is difficult to predict using stoichiometry.
L67 & 202. Citation is needed for the data set.
L71–72. This has been pointed out repeatedly by the previous studies.
L72–73. I think this statement is appropriate only when a certain time scale is considered. It is possible that N2O in the layer below the “source-sink” boundary could be ultimately released to the atmosphere by the global thermohaline circulation of deep water as speculated by Toyoda et al. (2019).
L79. Where is “the Northern Ocean”?
L80–82. Even above the oxycline, N2O can be produced by nitrification in the bottom of euphotic layer, and was suggested as a potential source to the atmosphere (Popp et al., 2002).
L84–86. The quantitative relationship between d18O and d15N of N2O in the anaerobic seawater has been already reported by Yamagishi et al. (2007).
L136–139. Without detailed information on the source-partitioning procedure and in situ reduced sulfur concentrations, I cannot believe the contribution of ADN as high as 13%. Did the authors test the calculation excluding ADN? I think a different solution can be obtained with mixing of four endmembers (AOA, AOB, HDN, and NDN).
L162–164. Citation is needed.
L201–202. Don’t the authors consider the seasonal variation in the N2O flux? I think most of the observational data were obtained at specific date/month/year. Seasonal variation has been suggested by studies based on data synthesis (Yang et al., 2020) and observation (Toyoda et al., 2023).
L223–225. This has been pointed out repeatedly by the previous studies.
L239. This holds under several assumptions as discussed by the previous studies.
L244–247. Cite appropriate references.
L277–279. Explain in detail. Did the authors use constant value for rN2O? Why?
L290. Explain the abbreviation at its first appearance.
L314. What do the authors mean by “concentration of the isotope”? Is it the isotope ratio?
L333–334. Didn’t the authors account for assimilation of ammonia by primary producers?
Supplement
L99. Where were the water and sediment collected?
Table S1. The epsilon and d15NSP values for ADN are different from those presented in L116. Explain the reason.
Table S2. Show uncertainty of the contributions.
L148. Is the “external input” of NH4 is included in the first term of the righthand side of the equation? If so, why it can be expressed by diffusion?
L149, 150, & 151. The sign of the second terms in the righthand side of the equations should be “+” because these express production of NO2/NO3/N2.
Figure S22. Cite the references used to create “observed” map. It is not clear what the “quantile” means. Was the distribution of the data with respect to their N2O concentration/flux divided into 10 groups?

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The ocean is the largest source of N2O emissions from global aquatic ecosystems. However, the N2O production–consumption mechanism and microbial spatial distribution are still unclear. Our study established a bottom-up model based on the source‒sink boundary and the microbial sources of N2O. A high-resolution (0.1°) global distribution of oceanic N2O was depicted, confirmed by approximately 150,000 surface measurements. The microbial N2O flux is 2.9 Tg/yr N-N2O, with the oxygen-deficient zones (ODZs) disproportionately accounting for more than half of the total emission. High primary productivity, sharp oxyclines, and shallow emission depths caused the ODZs to be N2O hotspots. Geographically, ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA, 1.0 Tg) are the most widely distributed contributors to N2O emissions in the ocean, completely overtaking ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB). Heterotrophic denitrification, mainly occurring in ODZs, contributes the most (1.6 Tg) to N2O emissions. Overall, this study offers a bottom-up framework for understanding microbial source-sink mechanism in the ocean.

---

## Introduction

Nitrous oxide (N2O), one of the most important greenhouse gases and the greatest human-related threat to the ozone layer, has increased substantially, by over 23%, since preindustrial times1. As a long-lived (116±9 years) greenhouse gas, nitrous oxide (N2O) is 265-298 times higher than CO2 in the global warming potential on a 100-year timescale2. Oceans are among Earth’s largest sources of N2O emissions, second only to natural soils and agriculture (IPCC). Although the amount of oceanic emissions has been well constrained3,4, current estimates are usually based on air‒sea flux (ΔpN2O)3,5 or simple semi-empirical equations6–8; thus, the N2O production‒consumption mechanism and spatial distribution of microbial N2O sources in oxygen-stratified oceans are still unclear9,10.

N2O emissions are microbially driven and highly oxygen sensitive in the ocean, leading to high heterogeneity in ΔpN2O. However, the coverage of ΔpN2O data is generally limited and in broad ranges, uncertainties inevitably widen when extrapolating ΔpN2O data to the global scale3. Moreover, sources and sinks coexist in the oxygen-stratified ocean11–13, and surface-based measurements cannot reflect the production and consumption of N2O in the deep layers. Therefore, how N2O is emitted from the ocean, how deep the source‒sink boundary is, and how it evolves cannot be explained, especially under the effects of increased stratification and deoxygenation expansion14. Most quantitative analyses of N2O microbial sources are conducted at the regional scale11,12 or on the basis of semi empirical equations of nitrification and denitrification6–8,10, which do not consider the niche separation of N2O-related microbial processes in different ecological niches6–8. For example, ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA) have greater affinity for substrates and compete for ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB) in the NH4+-limited ocean15,16. Nevertheless, several studies have reported the contribution of AOB to marine N2O emissions via nitrifier denitrification (NDN)17. Under hypoxic or anoxic conditions, N2O is produced as an intermediate during heterotrophic denitrification (HDN), with organic matter as the electron donor10,18. However, the quantification and spatial distributions of these microbes with respect to N2O emissions have not been well depicted in the ocean9,10.

In this study, we established a bottom-up model based on the source‒sink boundary and the microbial sources of marine N2O. Extensive literature research has been conducted to obtain the geochemical profiles of DO and N2O concentrations and isotopic signatures (δ15NBulk, δ18O and δ15NSP) at in situ locations (approximately 1000 lines of data), along with the isotopic characteristic values for each N2O production pathway (i.e., AOA, AOB, HDN, and NDN). We identified the source‒sink boundary of N2O via global oxygen stratification (up to 5000 m) in the water column. FRAME model was then used to quantify the specific microbial contributions to N2O emissions and N2O reduction degree19. Finally, the ammoxidation (ammonia oxidation) flux, N2O yield during ammoxidation (NO-N/NH4+-N), and quantified N2O microbial sources and fraction of residual unreduced N2O (rN2O) were combined as constraints to accurately estimate global marine N2O emissions. The results have been confirmed by a large compilation of N2O in situ measurements (approximately 150,000)3. Overall, our results present a detailed spatial distribution of marine N2O emissions with a source‒sink mechanism and quantified microbial sources.

---

## Results

N2O source‒sink boundary in the ocean
Due to the limit of light, the decomposition of organic matter or the poor mixing and ventilation, the ocean is oxygen-stratified. Earlier studies have revealed maximum N2O concentration in the oxygen minimum zones of the ocean11,20,21. N2O has a perfect mirror-image relationship with DO and reaches its highest concentration at the lowest amount of dissolved oxygen (Supplementary Figs. 2–11)11,22. Regardless of the upwelling, the source‒sink boundary of N2O, below which the water column does not contribute to N2O emissions, was identified by a comprehensive grid-by-grid (0.1°) traversal of DO up to 5000 m in the ocean (Fig. 1). In oxygen-deficient zones (ODZs), DO decreases to anaerobic levels (minimum O2 ≤10 μM) at shallower depths (387.9 m on average, Fig. 1b). In addition to the three major ODZs (Fig. 1c), namely, the Eastern Tropical North Pacific (ETNP), Eastern Tropical South Pacific (ETSP), and Arabian Sea, we also found some sporadic ODZs in the North Pacific Ocean, indicating the potential hotspots of N2O emissions. The upper oxycline (UO), with a N2O peak at the oxic‒anoxic interface (Supplementary Fig. 2–5), is the engine driving N2O diffusion to the mixed layer (ML). The sharp oxycline creates favorable conditions for incomplete denitrification and nitrification with high N2O yields, driving high supersaturation and fluxes of N2O at the surface11,23. Additionally, a stable proportionality of 0.45 and 2.58 for the plot of δ18O versus δ15NBulk (R2=0.52, Supplementary Fig. 12) was observed above and below the source‒sink boundary, respectively. In general, a strong correlation with slopes of 2.6 is evident when reduction process dominates, which contrasts from a slope of <1 commonly observed for mixing of N2O production and atmospheric N2O24–26. The slope of 0.45 proved the production, mixing and emission of N2O in the source part. In contrast, the slope of 2.58 confirmed the significant net N2O consumption in the ODZ core. Thereby the N2O concentrations simultaneously decreased to 0 at the middle of ODZ core (Fig. 1a). Furthermore, the isotopic composition of N2O in the ODZ core is significantly different from that in the source layer, further ruling out vertical exchange with the source layer. Therefore, the long-term and large-scale anaerobic areas ensure net N2O consumption in the ODZ core, which acts as the sink of N2O. In other oceans, the N2O peak was also observed at the lowest point of oxygen (Supplementary Fig. 6–11), although the boundary DO ranged from 10 μM to more than 300 μM (Fig. 1c). In the vast North Pacific Ocean and equatorial regions, the boundary DO is less than 50 μM, accompanied by a shallow boundary depth (less than 1000 m), favouring excessive N2O production and emission. A deeper source‒sink boundary has been found in the North Atlantic and Southern Oceans. The boundary DO increased to more than 300 μM with the boundary depth reaching 2000 m. Overall, the source‒sink boundary of N2O in the ocean was identified (Fig. 1), and the water column below the source‒sink boundary does not contribute to atmospheric emissions; therefore, it was excluded from the remainder of this study.

Microbial processes governing N2O production and consumption
To quantify the microbial sources of N2O and the fraction of residual unreduced N2O (rN2O) in the source part, the isotopic N2O values obtained from Keeling plot (Supplementary Figs. 13–22), the corrected isotope signatures of the microbial sources (Supplementary Table 1-2), and the isotopocule fractionation constants (i.e., εN: −15.4±4.7, εO: −7.1±2.1, and εSP: −5.9±1.4) for N2O reduction process were input to the model FRAME (Supplementary Fig. 23). In this study, four common microbial sources (HDN, NDN, AOB, AOA) and rN2O was quantified (Supplementary Fig. 24, Supplementary Table 3). The linear regression relationships between N2O microbial sources and boundary DO were uniformly adopted for extrapolation to global oceans (Supplementary Fig. 25, Fig. 2).

The primary productivity, substrate availability, boundary depth, and DO together determine the niche distribution of each N-cycling microorganism in the ocean. AOA dominate the nitrification pathway, contributing 34.1% of the N2O in the ocean (Table 1), which is the dominant N2O production pathway in the North Atlantic and Southern Oceans. Although both of them are chemoautotrophic processes, AOA have a greater affinity for NH4+ and oxygen20,22,27. Thereby, AOA exceeds AOB in NH4+-limited oceans with sharp oxyclines, while the contribution of AOB increases in high-latitude regions with high-oxygen (e.g., the Arctic Ocean and Antarctic Oceans). The isotopic signatures of N2O in the Arctic Ocean have proved the important role of both AOA and AOB to N2O productions12. In the ODZs, AOB are completely depleted (2.2%) because of phytoplankton competition, rapidly decreasing oxygen gradients, and surface light inhibition derived from shallow boundary depths. HDN, fueled by organic matter exported from the photic zone, is the dominant N2O production pathway in the North Pacific Ocean and equatorial regions. It further increases to 63.3% in ODZs because the abundant organic electron donors and sharp oxyclines create favorable conditions for incomplete denitrification. Notably, the contribution of denitrification is still considerable even if DO does not reach the anaerobic level in the open ocean. It is possibly associated with organic particles; the interior of sinking particles can afford a low-DO microenvironment20. On a global scale (Fig. 2), the contribution of denitrification (HDN+NDN) to N2O emissions is 61.1% (Table 1), nearly two-fold greater than that of nitrification (AOA+AOB). HDN is the first contributor to oceanic N2O emission, whereas AOA are the most widely distributed contributor in the ocean.

Global distribution of N2O flux in the ocean
To obtain the global N2O flux in a year scale (Tg N2O-N/yr), we first calculated the N2O emissions by AOA (N2OAOA) in each grid on the basis of the ammoxidation flux (ammonia oxidation amount in a year scale), N2O yield during ammoxidation (NO-N/NH4+-N), and the fraction of residual unreduced N2O (rN2O, Supplementary Fig. 25e). The total N2O flux was then obtained according to its proportion to total production in each grid (e.g., N2OAOA/fAOA; see Methods for details). It is worth noting that the fraction of residual unreduced N2O (rN2O) determines the net emission of N2O. We established the empirical formula between the rN2O and the boundary DO (Supplementary Fig. 25e). As the boundary DO rises, there is initially an increase in rN2O, followed by a subsequent decline. In ODZs with micro-oxic environment, the N2O production and reduction are both active. As the boundary DO increases, the N2O reduction is prior to be inhibited as nitrous oxide reductase (nos) is the most O2 sensitive denitrifying enzyme28, leading to the increase of rN2O. However, the data obtained in the shallow Arctic Ocean and off the coast of Antarctica gave rN2O values as low as 20% in spite of high boundary DO (Supplementary Fig. 25e)3,12,29. This implies that a significant portion of the N2O produced in situ or diffused from the atmosphere is reduced by denitrification in sediments12.

The annual N2O flux is 2.9 Tg/yr N-N2O (Fig. 3, Table 1), the distribution of which is in line with primary production pulses. On average, the turnover rate of phytoplankton (growth, death, and mineralization) is 45 times a year30, providing never-ending NH4+, NO3-, and organic matter for the continuous production of N2O via nitrification and denitrification. Furthermore, the decay of phytoplankton creates the anaerobic environment for the significant production of N2O. Therefore, the oceans around the equator contribute the most to marine N2O emissions, where ODZs disproportionately account for more than half of N2O emissions (1.6 Tg N-N2O) with only 0.1–0.2% of the ocean volume31. A higher flux of N2O has also been observed in other oceans with high primary productivity, e.g., the Gulf of Guinea, Bay of Bengal, Gulf of Mexico, and Indonesia. In contrast, slight supersaturation and occasional undersaturation are predicted in the open Arctic Ocean and Southern Ocean, with limits on light and temperature at high latitudes. With respect to microbial sources (Table 1), the contribution of denitrification is almost twofold greater than that of nitrification. Traditional HDN is the largest contributor (1.6 Tg) to N2O emissions in the ocean, which mainly occurs in ODZs (1.0 Tg). AOA are the most widely distributed contributors (1.0 Tg) in the NH4+-limited ocean and completely overcome AOB (0.1 Tg) to N2O emissions.

### Reviewer 3

General comments
This paper reports detailed estimates of oceanic N2O flux and relative contributions of biological N2O production processes using published data of N2O isotope ratios, basic physical and chemical oceanic parameters, and a three-dimensional diffusion and reaction model. Because the ocean is one of the major sources of N2O, a potent greenhouse gas as well as a stratospheric ozone depleting gas, improving the estimates of N2O flux and understanding the key N2O production mechanisms would be beneficial in predicting future increases or decreases in N2O concentrations.
The strength of this paper is that the N2O flux was estimated with high spatial resolution using relatively basic parameters such as temperature, dissolved oxygen, particular organic nitrogen with the aid of N2O isotope ratios that provide a history of microbial production and consumption processes. The model-predicted N2O flux well reproduces spatial gradient found by observations.
However, this paper has several shortcomings. First, the developed method for calculating the N2O flux depends on source partitioning based on isotopic measurements that cover only a few specific regions in the global ocean. For example, the authors used isotopic data from only eastern parts of the North and South Pacific. I think there have been several reports on other parts of the Pacific. Although the authors argue that relative contribution of nitrification and DO at the “source-sink” boundary has a linear relationship, it is not necessarily proven by the data presented in Figure S20. I think examination of more data from other regions are necessary.
Second, the authors’ assumption that N2O dissolved in the depths shallower than the “source-sink” boundary is a simple mixture of two components, N2O of atmospheric origin and that produced near the boundary, is a crude one that ignores detailed analysis of previous studies. For example, Kelly et al. (2021) identified two sources between the surface and the near-surface N2O maximum in their Keeling plot analysis of isotopic data obtained in the ETNP results. Toyoda et al. (2002) also noted that there are two different N2O sources between the surface and N2O maximum in the western North Pacific, although the latter work is not referred in the present manuscript. In addition to these points, I have a concern that previous efforts on observations and interpretation of oceanic N2O are not fully acknowledged in this manuscript.
Third, it is not clear whether the authors assume the occurrence of N2O reduction even in the shallower seawater above the “source-sink” boundary. I was not able to understand why they uniformly used rN2O = 0.72 to estimate isotopic signature of N2O produced by microbial processes even though they seem to define the upper layer as source region.
Fourth, uncertainty of the estimated contributions from each microbial process is not shown, and explanation of the isotope-based source partitioning procedure is missing both in text and supporting materials. I cannot evaluate the accuracy of the estimation.
In summary, I do not recommend the publication of this paper in its present form. I encourage the authors to address the issue above and specific points below.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

The ocean is the largest source of N2O emissions from global aquatic ecosystems. However, the N2O production–consumption mechanism and microbial spatial distribution are still unclear. Our study established a bottom-up model based on the source‒sink boundary and the microbial sources of N2O. A high-resolution (0.1°) global distribution of oceanic N2O was depicted, confirmed by approximately 150,000 surface measurements. The microbial N2O flux is 2.9 Tg/yr N-N2O, with the oxygen-deficient zones (ODZs) disproportionately accounting for more than half of the total emission. High primary productivity, sharp oxyclines, and shallow emission depths caused the ODZs to be N2O hotspots. Geographically, ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA, 1.0 Tg) are the most widely distributed contributors to N2O emissions in the ocean, completely overtaking ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB). Heterotrophic denitrification, mainly occurring in ODZs, contributes the most (1.6 Tg) to N2O emissions. Overall, this study offers a bottom-up framework for understanding microbial source-sink mechanism in the ocean.

---

## Introduction

Nitrous oxide (N2O), one of the most important greenhouse gases and the greatest human-related threat to the ozone layer, has increased substantially, by over 23%, since preindustrial times1. As a long-lived (116±9 years) greenhouse gas, nitrous oxide (N2O) is 265-298 times higher than CO2 in the global warming potential on a 100-year timescale2. Oceans are among Earth’s largest sources of N2O emissions, second only to natural soils and agriculture (IPCC). Although the amount of oceanic emissions has been well constrained3,4, current estimates are usually based on air‒sea flux (ΔpN2O)3,5 or simple semi-empirical equations6–8; thus, the N2O production‒consumption mechanism and spatial distribution of microbial N2O sources in oxygen-stratified oceans are still unclear9,10.

N2O emissions are microbially driven and highly oxygen sensitive in the ocean, leading to high heterogeneity in ΔpN2O. However, the coverage of ΔpN2O data is generally limited and in broad ranges, uncertainties inevitably widen when extrapolating ΔpN2O data to the global scale3. Moreover, sources and sinks coexist in the oxygen-stratified ocean11–13, and surface-based measurements cannot reflect the production and consumption of N2O in the deep layers. Therefore, how N2O is emitted from the ocean, how deep the source‒sink boundary is, and how it evolves cannot be explained, especially under the effects of increased stratification and deoxygenation expansion14. Most quantitative analyses of N2O microbial sources are conducted at the regional scale11,12 or on the basis of semi empirical equations of nitrification and denitrification6–8,10, which do not consider the niche separation of N2O-related microbial processes in different ecological niches6–8. For example, ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA) have greater affinity for substrates and compete for ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB) in the NH4+-limited ocean15,16. Nevertheless, several studies have reported the contribution of AOB to marine N2O emissions via nitrifier denitrification (NDN)17. Under hypoxic or anoxic conditions, N2O is produced as an intermediate during heterotrophic denitrification (HDN), with organic matter as the electron donor10,18. However, the quantification and spatial distributions of these microbes with respect to N2O emissions have not been well depicted in the ocean9,10.

In this study, we established a bottom-up model based on the source‒sink boundary and the microbial sources of marine N2O. Extensive literature research has been conducted to obtain the geochemical profiles of DO and N2O concentrations and isotopic signatures (δ15NBulk, δ18O and δ15NSP) at in situ locations (approximately 1000 lines of data), along with the isotopic characteristic values for each N2O production pathway (i.e., AOA, AOB, HDN, and NDN). We identified the source‒sink boundary of N2O via global oxygen stratification (up to 5000 m) in the water column. FRAME model was then used to quantify the specific microbial contributions to N2O emissions and N2O reduction degree19. Finally, the ammoxidation (ammonia oxidation) flux, N2O yield during ammoxidation (NO-N/NH4+-N), and quantified N2O microbial sources and fraction of residual unreduced N2O (rN2O) were combined as constraints to accurately estimate global marine N2O emissions. The results have been confirmed by a large compilation of N2O in situ measurements (approximately 150,000)3. Overall, our results present a detailed spatial distribution of marine N2O emissions with a source‒sink mechanism and quantified microbial sources.

---

## Results

N2O source‒sink boundary in the ocean
Due to the limit of light, the decomposition of organic matter or the poor mixing and ventilation, the ocean is oxygen-stratified. Earlier studies have revealed maximum N2O concentration in the oxygen minimum zones of the ocean11,20,21. N2O has a perfect mirror-image relationship with DO and reaches its highest concentration at the lowest amount of dissolved oxygen (Supplementary Figs. 2–11)11,22. Regardless of the upwelling, the source‒sink boundary of N2O, below which the water column does not contribute to N2O emissions, was identified by a comprehensive grid-by-grid (0.1°) traversal of DO up to 5000 m in the ocean (Fig. 1). In oxygen-deficient zones (ODZs), DO decreases to anaerobic levels (minimum O2 ≤10 μM) at shallower depths (387.9 m on average, Fig. 1b). In addition to the three major ODZs (Fig. 1c), namely, the Eastern Tropical North Pacific (ETNP), Eastern Tropical South Pacific (ETSP), and Arabian Sea, we also found some sporadic ODZs in the North Pacific Ocean, indicating the potential hotspots of N2O emissions. The upper oxycline (UO), with a N2O peak at the oxic‒anoxic interface (Supplementary Fig. 2–5), is the engine driving N2O diffusion to the mixed layer (ML). The sharp oxycline creates favorable conditions for incomplete denitrification and nitrification with high N2O yields, driving high supersaturation and fluxes of N2O at the surface11,23. Additionally, a stable proportionality of 0.45 and 2.58 for the plot of δ18O versus δ15NBulk (R2=0.52, Supplementary Fig. 12) was observed above and below the source‒sink boundary, respectively. In general, a strong correlation with slopes of 2.6 is evident when reduction process dominates, which contrasts from a slope of <1 commonly observed for mixing of N2O production and atmospheric N2O24–26. The slope of 0.45 proved the production, mixing and emission of N2O in the source part. In contrast, the slope of 2.58 confirmed the significant net N2O consumption in the ODZ core. Thereby the N2O concentrations simultaneously decreased to 0 at the middle of ODZ core (Fig. 1a). Furthermore, the isotopic composition of N2O in the ODZ core is significantly different from that in the source layer, further ruling out vertical exchange with the source layer. Therefore, the long-term and large-scale anaerobic areas ensure net N2O consumption in the ODZ core, which acts as the sink of N2O. In other oceans, the N2O peak was also observed at the lowest point of oxygen (Supplementary Fig. 6–11), although the boundary DO ranged from 10 μM to more than 300 μM (Fig. 1c). In the vast North Pacific Ocean and equatorial regions, the boundary DO is less than 50 μM, accompanied by a shallow boundary depth (less than 1000 m), favouring excessive N2O production and emission. A deeper source‒sink boundary has been found in the North Atlantic and Southern Oceans. The boundary DO increased to more than 300 μM with the boundary depth reaching 2000 m. Overall, the source‒sink boundary of N2O in the ocean was identified (Fig. 1), and the water column below the source‒sink boundary does not contribute to atmospheric emissions; therefore, it was excluded from the remainder of this study.

Microbial processes governing N2O production and consumption
To quantify the microbial sources of N2O and the fraction of residual unreduced N2O (rN2O) in the source part, the isotopic N2O values obtained from Keeling plot (Supplementary Figs. 13–22), the corrected isotope signatures of the microbial sources (Supplementary Table 1-2), and the isotopocule fractionation constants (i.e., εN: −15.4±4.7, εO: −7.1±2.1, and εSP: −5.9±1.4) for N2O reduction process were input to the model FRAME (Supplementary Fig. 23). In this study, four common microbial sources (HDN, NDN, AOB, AOA) and rN2O was quantified (Supplementary Fig. 24, Supplementary Table 3). The linear regression relationships between N2O microbial sources and boundary DO were uniformly adopted for extrapolation to global oceans (Supplementary Fig. 25, Fig. 2).

The primary productivity, substrate availability, boundary depth, and DO together determine the niche distribution of each N-cycling microorganism in the ocean. AOA dominate the nitrification pathway, contributing 34.1% of the N2O in the ocean (Table 1), which is the dominant N2O production pathway in the North Atlantic and Southern Oceans. Although both of them are chemoautotrophic processes, AOA have a greater affinity for NH4+ and oxygen20,22,27. Thereby, AOA exceeds AOB in NH4+-limited oceans with sharp oxyclines, while the contribution of AOB increases in high-latitude regions with high-oxygen (e.g., the Arctic Ocean and Antarctic Oceans). The isotopic signatures of N2O in the Arctic Ocean have proved the important role of both AOA and AOB to N2O productions12. In the ODZs, AOB are completely depleted (2.2%) because of phytoplankton competition, rapidly decreasing oxygen gradients, and surface light inhibition derived from shallow boundary depths. HDN, fueled by organic matter exported from the photic zone, is the dominant N2O production pathway in the North Pacific Ocean and equatorial regions. It further increases to 63.3% in ODZs because the abundant organic electron donors and sharp oxyclines create favorable conditions for incomplete denitrification. Notably, the contribution of denitrification is still considerable even if DO does not reach the anaerobic level in the open ocean. It is possibly associated with organic particles; the interior of sinking particles can afford a low-DO microenvironment20. On a global scale (Fig. 2), the contribution of denitrification (HDN+NDN) to N2O emissions is 61.1% (Table 1), nearly two-fold greater than that of nitrification (AOA+AOB). HDN is the first contributor to oceanic N2O emission, whereas AOA are the most widely distributed contributor in the ocean.

Global distribution of N2O flux in the ocean
To obtain the global N2O flux in a year scale (Tg N2O-N/yr), we first calculated the N2O emissions by AOA (N2OAOA) in each grid on the basis of the ammoxidation flux (ammonia oxidation amount in a year scale), N2O yield during ammoxidation (NO-N/NH4+-N), and the fraction of residual unreduced N2O (rN2O, Supplementary Fig. 25e). The total N2O flux was then obtained according to its proportion to total production in each grid (e.g., N2OAOA/fAOA; see Methods for details). It is worth noting that the fraction of residual unreduced N2O (rN2O) determines the net emission of N2O. We established the empirical formula between the rN2O and the boundary DO (Supplementary Fig. 25e). As the boundary DO rises, there is initially an increase in rN2O, followed by a subsequent decline. In ODZs with micro-oxic environment, the N2O production and reduction are both active. As the boundary DO increases, the N2O reduction is prior to be inhibited as nitrous oxide reductase (nos) is the most O2 sensitive denitrifying enzyme28, leading to the increase of rN2O. However, the data obtained in the shallow Arctic Ocean and off the coast of Antarctica gave rN2O values as low as 20% in spite of high boundary DO (Supplementary Fig. 25e)3,12,29. This implies that a significant portion of the N2O produced in situ or diffused from the atmosphere is reduced by denitrification in sediments12.

The annual N2O flux is 2.9 Tg/yr N-N2O (Fig. 3, Table 1), the distribution of which is in line with primary production pulses. On average, the turnover rate of phytoplankton (growth, death, and mineralization) is 45 times a year30, providing never-ending NH4+, NO3-, and organic matter for the continuous production of N2O via nitrification and denitrification. Furthermore, the decay of phytoplankton creates the anaerobic environment for the significant production of N2O. Therefore, the oceans around the equator contribute the most to marine N2O emissions, where ODZs disproportionately account for more than half of N2O emissions (1.6 Tg N-N2O) with only 0.1–0.2% of the ocean volume31. A higher flux of N2O has also been observed in other oceans with high primary productivity, e.g., the Gulf of Guinea, Bay of Bengal, Gulf of Mexico, and Indonesia. In contrast, slight supersaturation and occasional undersaturation are predicted in the open Arctic Ocean and Southern Ocean, with limits on light and temperature at high latitudes. With respect to microbial sources (Table 1), the contribution of denitrification is almost twofold greater than that of nitrification. Traditional HDN is the largest contributor (1.6 Tg) to N2O emissions in the ocean, which mainly occurs in ODZs (1.0 Tg). AOA are the most widely distributed contributors (1.0 Tg) in the NH4+-limited ocean and completely overcome AOB (0.1 Tg) to N2O emissions.

### Reviewer 3

General comments
This paper reports detailed estimates of oceanic N2O flux and relative contributions of biological N2O production processes using published data of N2O isotope ratios, basic physical and chemical oceanic parameters, and a three-dimensional diffusion and reaction model. Because the ocean is one of the major sources of N2O, a potent greenhouse gas as well as a stratospheric ozone depleting gas, improving the estimates of N2O flux and understanding the key N2O production mechanisms would be beneficial in predicting future increases or decreases in N2O concentrations.
The strength of this paper is that the N2O flux was estimated with high spatial resolution using relatively basic parameters such as temperature, dissolved oxygen, particular organic nitrogen with the aid of N2O isotope ratios that provide a history of microbial production and consumption processes. The model-predicted N2O flux well reproduces spatial gradient found by observations.
However, this paper has several shortcomings. First, the developed method for calculating the N2O flux depends on source partitioning based on isotopic measurements that cover only a few specific regions in the global ocean. For example, the authors used isotopic data from only eastern parts of the North and South Pacific. I think there have been several reports on other parts of the Pacific. Although the authors argue that relative contribution of nitrification and DO at the “source-sink” boundary has a linear relationship, it is not necessarily proven by the data presented in Figure S20. I think examination of more data from other regions are necessary.
Second, the authors’ assumption that N2O dissolved in the depths shallower than the “source-sink” boundary is a simple mixture of two components, N2O of atmospheric origin and that produced near the boundary, is a crude one that ignores detailed analysis of previous studies. For example, Kelly et al. (2021) identified two sources between the surface and the near-surface N2O maximum in their Keeling plot analysis of isotopic data obtained in the ETNP results. Toyoda et al. (2002) also noted that there are two different N2O sources between the surface and N2O maximum in the western North Pacific, although the latter work is not referred in the present manuscript. In addition to these points, I have a concern that previous efforts on observations and interpretation of oceanic N2O are not fully acknowledged in this manuscript.
Third, it is not clear whether the authors assume the occurrence of N2O reduction even in the shallower seawater above the “source-sink” boundary. I was not able to understand why they uniformly used rN2O = 0.72 to estimate isotopic signature of N2O produced by microbial processes even though they seem to define the upper layer as source region.
Fourth, uncertainty of the estimated contributions from each microbial process is not shown, and explanation of the isotope-based source partitioning procedure is missing both in text and supporting materials. I cannot evaluate the accuracy of the estimation.
In summary, I do not recommend the publication of this paper in its present form. I encourage the authors to address the issue above and specific points below.

## Paper

## Abstract

The ocean is the largest source of N2O emissions from global aquatic ecosystems. However, the N2O production–consumption mechanism and microbial spatial distribution are still unclear. Our study established a bottom-up model based on the source‒sink boundary and the microbial sources of N2O. A high-resolution (0.1°) global distribution of oceanic N2O was depicted, confirmed by approximately 150,000 surface measurements. The microbial N2O flux is 2.9 Tg/yr N-N2O, with the oxygen-deficient zones (ODZs) disproportionately accounting for more than half of the total emission. High primary productivity, sharp oxyclines, and shallow emission depths caused the ODZs to be N2O hotspots. Geographically, ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA, 1.0 Tg) are the most widely distributed contributors to N2O emissions in the ocean, completely overtaking ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB). Heterotrophic denitrification, mainly occurring in ODZs, contributes the most (1.6 Tg) to N2O emissions. Overall, this study offers a bottom-up framework for understanding microbial source-sink mechanism in the ocean.

---

## Introduction

Nitrous oxide (N2O), one of the most important greenhouse gases and the greatest human-related threat to the ozone layer, has increased substantially, by over 23%, since preindustrial times1. As a long-lived (116±9 years) greenhouse gas, nitrous oxide (N2O) is 265-298 times higher than CO2 in the global warming potential on a 100-year timescale2. Oceans are among Earth’s largest sources of N2O emissions, second only to natural soils and agriculture (IPCC). Although the amount of oceanic emissions has been well constrained3,4, current estimates are usually based on air‒sea flux (ΔpN2O)3,5 or simple semi-empirical equations6–8; thus, the N2O production‒consumption mechanism and spatial distribution of microbial N2O sources in oxygen-stratified oceans are still unclear9,10.

N2O emissions are microbially driven and highly oxygen sensitive in the ocean, leading to high heterogeneity in ΔpN2O. However, the coverage of ΔpN2O data is generally limited and in broad ranges, uncertainties inevitably widen when extrapolating ΔpN2O data to the global scale3. Moreover, sources and sinks coexist in the oxygen-stratified ocean11–13, and surface-based measurements cannot reflect the production and consumption of N2O in the deep layers. Therefore, how N2O is emitted from the ocean, how deep the source‒sink boundary is, and how it evolves cannot be explained, especially under the effects of increased stratification and deoxygenation expansion14. Most quantitative analyses of N2O microbial sources are conducted at the regional scale11,12 or on the basis of semi empirical equations of nitrification and denitrification6–8,10, which do not consider the niche separation of N2O-related microbial processes in different ecological niches6–8. For example, ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA) have greater affinity for substrates and compete for ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB) in the NH4+-limited ocean15,16. Nevertheless, several studies have reported the contribution of AOB to marine N2O emissions via nitrifier denitrification (NDN)17. Under hypoxic or anoxic conditions, N2O is produced as an intermediate during heterotrophic denitrification (HDN), with organic matter as the electron donor10,18. However, the quantification and spatial distributions of these microbes with respect to N2O emissions have not been well depicted in the ocean9,10.

In this study, we established a bottom-up model based on the source‒sink boundary and the microbial sources of marine N2O. Extensive literature research has been conducted to obtain the geochemical profiles of DO and N2O concentrations and isotopic signatures (δ15NBulk, δ18O and δ15NSP) at in situ locations (approximately 1000 lines of data), along with the isotopic characteristic values for each N2O production pathway (i.e., AOA, AOB, HDN, and NDN). We identified the source‒sink boundary of N2O via global oxygen stratification (up to 5000 m) in the water column. FRAME model was then used to quantify the specific microbial contributions to N2O emissions and N2O reduction degree19. Finally, the ammoxidation (ammonia oxidation) flux, N2O yield during ammoxidation (NO-N/NH4+-N), and quantified N2O microbial sources and fraction of residual unreduced N2O (rN2O) were combined as constraints to accurately estimate global marine N2O emissions. The results have been confirmed by a large compilation of N2O in situ measurements (approximately 150,000)3. Overall, our results present a detailed spatial distribution of marine N2O emissions with a source‒sink mechanism and quantified microbial sources.

---

## Results

N2O source‒sink boundary in the ocean
Due to the limit of light, the decomposition of organic matter or the poor mixing and ventilation, the ocean is oxygen-stratified. Earlier studies have revealed maximum N2O concentration in the oxygen minimum zones of the ocean11,20,21. N2O has a perfect mirror-image relationship with DO and reaches its highest concentration at the lowest amount of dissolved oxygen (Supplementary Figs. 2–11)11,22. Regardless of the upwelling, the source‒sink boundary of N2O, below which the water column does not contribute to N2O emissions, was identified by a comprehensive grid-by-grid (0.1°) traversal of DO up to 5000 m in the ocean (Fig. 1). In oxygen-deficient zones (ODZs), DO decreases to anaerobic levels (minimum O2 ≤10 μM) at shallower depths (387.9 m on average, Fig. 1b). In addition to the three major ODZs (Fig. 1c), namely, the Eastern Tropical North Pacific (ETNP), Eastern Tropical South Pacific (ETSP), and Arabian Sea, we also found some sporadic ODZs in the North Pacific Ocean, indicating the potential hotspots of N2O emissions. The upper oxycline (UO), with a N2O peak at the oxic‒anoxic interface (Supplementary Fig. 2–5), is the engine driving N2O diffusion to the mixed layer (ML). The sharp oxycline creates favorable conditions for incomplete denitrification and nitrification with high N2O yields, driving high supersaturation and fluxes of N2O at the surface11,23. Additionally, a stable proportionality of 0.45 and 2.58 for the plot of δ18O versus δ15NBulk (R2=0.52, Supplementary Fig. 12) was observed above and below the source‒sink boundary, respectively. In general, a strong correlation with slopes of 2.6 is evident when reduction process dominates, which contrasts from a slope of <1 commonly observed for mixing of N2O production and atmospheric N2O24–26. The slope of 0.45 proved the production, mixing and emission of N2O in the source part. In contrast, the slope of 2.58 confirmed the significant net N2O consumption in the ODZ core. Thereby the N2O concentrations simultaneously decreased to 0 at the middle of ODZ core (Fig. 1a). Furthermore, the isotopic composition of N2O in the ODZ core is significantly different from that in the source layer, further ruling out vertical exchange with the source layer. Therefore, the long-term and large-scale anaerobic areas ensure net N2O consumption in the ODZ core, which acts as the sink of N2O. In other oceans, the N2O peak was also observed at the lowest point of oxygen (Supplementary Fig. 6–11), although the boundary DO ranged from 10 μM to more than 300 μM (Fig. 1c). In the vast North Pacific Ocean and equatorial regions, the boundary DO is less than 50 μM, accompanied by a shallow boundary depth (less than 1000 m), favouring excessive N2O production and emission. A deeper source‒sink boundary has been found in the North Atlantic and Southern Oceans. The boundary DO increased to more than 300 μM with the boundary depth reaching 2000 m. Overall, the source‒sink boundary of N2O in the ocean was identified (Fig. 1), and the water column below the source‒sink boundary does not contribute to atmospheric emissions; therefore, it was excluded from the remainder of this study.

Microbial processes governing N2O production and consumption
To quantify the microbial sources of N2O and the fraction of residual unreduced N2O (rN2O) in the source part, the isotopic N2O values obtained from Keeling plot (Supplementary Figs. 13–22), the corrected isotope signatures of the microbial sources (Supplementary Table 1-2), and the isotopocule fractionation constants (i.e., εN: −15.4±4.7, εO: −7.1±2.1, and εSP: −5.9±1.4) for N2O reduction process were input to the model FRAME (Supplementary Fig. 23). In this study, four common microbial sources (HDN, NDN, AOB, AOA) and rN2O was quantified (Supplementary Fig. 24, Supplementary Table 3). The linear regression relationships between N2O microbial sources and boundary DO were uniformly adopted for extrapolation to global oceans (Supplementary Fig. 25, Fig. 2).

The primary productivity, substrate availability, boundary depth, and DO together determine the niche distribution of each N-cycling microorganism in the ocean. AOA dominate the nitrification pathway, contributing 34.1% of the N2O in the ocean (Table 1), which is the dominant N2O production pathway in the North Atlantic and Southern Oceans. Although both of them are chemoautotrophic processes, AOA have a greater affinity for NH4+ and oxygen20,22,27. Thereby, AOA exceeds AOB in NH4+-limited oceans with sharp oxyclines, while the contribution of AOB increases in high-latitude regions with high-oxygen (e.g., the Arctic Ocean and Antarctic Oceans). The isotopic signatures of N2O in the Arctic Ocean have proved the important role of both AOA and AOB to N2O productions12. In the ODZs, AOB are completely depleted (2.2%) because of phytoplankton competition, rapidly decreasing oxygen gradients, and surface light inhibition derived from shallow boundary depths. HDN, fueled by organic matter exported from the photic zone, is the dominant N2O production pathway in the North Pacific Ocean and equatorial regions. It further increases to 63.3% in ODZs because the abundant organic electron donors and sharp oxyclines create favorable conditions for incomplete denitrification. Notably, the contribution of denitrification is still considerable even if DO does not reach the anaerobic level in the open ocean. It is possibly associated with organic particles; the interior of sinking particles can afford a low-DO microenvironment20. On a global scale (Fig. 2), the contribution of denitrification (HDN+NDN) to N2O emissions is 61.1% (Table 1), nearly two-fold greater than that of nitrification (AOA+AOB). HDN is the first contributor to oceanic N2O emission, whereas AOA are the most widely distributed contributor in the ocean.

Global distribution of N2O flux in the ocean
To obtain the global N2O flux in a year scale (Tg N2O-N/yr), we first calculated the N2O emissions by AOA (N2OAOA) in each grid on the basis of the ammoxidation flux (ammonia oxidation amount in a year scale), N2O yield during ammoxidation (NO-N/NH4+-N), and the fraction of residual unreduced N2O (rN2O, Supplementary Fig. 25e). The total N2O flux was then obtained according to its proportion to total production in each grid (e.g., N2OAOA/fAOA; see Methods for details). It is worth noting that the fraction of residual unreduced N2O (rN2O) determines the net emission of N2O. We established the empirical formula between the rN2O and the boundary DO (Supplementary Fig. 25e). As the boundary DO rises, there is initially an increase in rN2O, followed by a subsequent decline. In ODZs with micro-oxic environment, the N2O production and reduction are both active. As the boundary DO increases, the N2O reduction is prior to be inhibited as nitrous oxide reductase (nos) is the most O2 sensitive denitrifying enzyme28, leading to the increase of rN2O. However, the data obtained in the shallow Arctic Ocean and off the coast of Antarctica gave rN2O values as low as 20% in spite of high boundary DO (Supplementary Fig. 25e)3,12,29. This implies that a significant portion of the N2O produced in situ or diffused from the atmosphere is reduced by denitrification in sediments12.

The annual N2O flux is 2.9 Tg/yr N-N2O (Fig. 3, Table 1), the distribution of which is in line with primary production pulses. On average, the turnover rate of phytoplankton (growth, death, and mineralization) is 45 times a year30, providing never-ending NH4+, NO3-, and organic matter for the continuous production of N2O via nitrification and denitrification. Furthermore, the decay of phytoplankton creates the anaerobic environment for the significant production of N2O. Therefore, the oceans around the equator contribute the most to marine N2O emissions, where ODZs disproportionately account for more than half of N2O emissions (1.6 Tg N-N2O) with only 0.1–0.2% of the ocean volume31. A higher flux of N2O has also been observed in other oceans with high primary productivity, e.g., the Gulf of Guinea, Bay of Bengal, Gulf of Mexico, and Indonesia. In contrast, slight supersaturation and occasional undersaturation are predicted in the open Arctic Ocean and Southern Ocean, with limits on light and temperature at high latitudes. With respect to microbial sources (Table 1), the contribution of denitrification is almost twofold greater than that of nitrification. Traditional HDN is the largest contributor (1.6 Tg) to N2O emissions in the ocean, which mainly occurs in ODZs (1.0 Tg). AOA are the most widely distributed contributors (1.0 Tg) in the NH4+-limited ocean and completely overcome AOB (0.1 Tg) to N2O emissions.

### Reviewer 3

General comments
This paper reports detailed estimates of oceanic N2O flux and relative contributions of biological N2O production processes using published data of N2O isotope ratios, basic physical and chemical oceanic parameters, and a three-dimensional diffusion and reaction model. Because the ocean is one of the major sources of N2O, a potent greenhouse gas as well as a stratospheric ozone depleting gas, improving the estimates of N2O flux and understanding the key N2O production mechanisms would be beneficial in predicting future increases or decreases in N2O concentrations.
The strength of this paper is that the N2O flux was estimated with high spatial resolution using relatively basic parameters such as temperature, dissolved oxygen, particular organic nitrogen with the aid of N2O isotope ratios that provide a history of microbial production and consumption processes. The model-predicted N2O flux well reproduces spatial gradient found by observations.
However, this paper has several shortcomings. First, the developed method for calculating the N2O flux depends on source partitioning based on isotopic measurements that cover only a few specific regions in the global ocean. For example, the authors used isotopic data from only eastern parts of the North and South Pacific. I think there have been several reports on other parts of the Pacific. Although the authors argue that relative contribution of nitrification and DO at the “source-sink” boundary has a linear relationship, it is not necessarily proven by the data presented in Figure S20. I think examination of more data from other regions are necessary.
Second, the authors’ assumption that N2O dissolved in the depths shallower than the “source-sink” boundary is a simple mixture of two components, N2O of atmospheric origin and that produced near the boundary, is a crude one that ignores detailed analysis of previous studies. For example, Kelly et al. (2021) identified two sources between the surface and the near-surface N2O maximum in their Keeling plot analysis of isotopic data obtained in the ETNP results. Toyoda et al. (2002) also noted that there are two different N2O sources between the surface and N2O maximum in the western North Pacific, although the latter work is not referred in the present manuscript. In addition to these points, I have a concern that previous efforts on observations and interpretation of oceanic N2O are not fully acknowledged in this manuscript.
Third, it is not clear whether the authors assume the occurrence of N2O reduction even in the shallower seawater above the “source-sink” boundary. I was not able to understand why they uniformly used rN2O = 0.72 to estimate isotopic signature of N2O produced by microbial processes even though they seem to define the upper layer as source region.
Fourth, uncertainty of the estimated contributions from each microbial process is not shown, and explanation of the isotope-based source partitioning procedure is missing both in text and supporting materials. I cannot evaluate the accuracy of the estimation.
In summary, I do not recommend the publication of this paper in its present form. I encourage the authors to address the issue above and specific points below.

Answer: Thanks for your comments. As δ15NBulk and δ18O are dependent on the substrates, we adopted corrected isotopic values to avoid bias from precursor substances(Lewicka-Szczebak et al., 2020; Lewicki et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2019). The precursor isotopic signatures (δ15N-PON, δ15N-NO -, and δ18O-H O) were taken into account in FRAME (Liang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2024b). Because it is rare to obtain the isotopic values of NH + due to its low concentrations in oceans, the nitrogen isotope of particulate organic nitrogen (PON) minus the isotope effect (ε , approximately -1‰) was used as the background isotope value of ammonia(Yoshikawa et al., 2016). The ε15NBulk, ε18O and δ15NSP values of N O for each process and substrates of N O (PON, NO − , or H O) were found in the literature (Table S1-S2). The literature endmember values are given as isotope effects (ε15NBulk, ε18O), ε = δ − δ . The input endmember values are corrected with the actually measured precursor values, δ = ε + δ . Specifically, the corrected δ15NBulk (‰) endmember values for AOA, AOB and NDN depend on the value of δ15N-PON + ε , whereas δ15NBulk (‰) for HDN, ADN depends on the value of δ15N-NO -. The δ18O endmember values for HDN, ADN and NDN depend on the δ18O-H O. The actual isotopic signatures of the substrate in each region are summarized in Table S2. (Line312-329)
Similar to previous literatures (Chen et al., 2023; Lewicka-Szczebak et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2022), oxygen isotope values of O 2 were not considered, thus we only consider the δ18O-H 2 O (‰) in this paper. The total N O flux was then obtained according to its proportion to total production in each grid (e.g., N O /f ).
